note: Editorial analysis questions maintained in this repository, grouped by issues shared across all approaches and issues specific to each approach. Each question includes its reasoning; the OSCAL examples provide evidence without settling the design choices.
intro: These questions identify unresolved design choices, not recommended changes. The analysis distinguishes what the OSCAL examples demonstrate from what remains open across models and approaches.

sections.label: Across all three approaches
sections.intro: Questions shared by all three approaches. None is answered by choosing an approach, and each affects how the resulting artifacts are interpreted.

questions.q: Should OSCAL carry this content at all, when XCCDF already does?
questions.why: XCCDF already represents benchmark checklists. OSCAL could carry equivalent content or connect checklist references to implementation and assessment records. These choices produce different artifacts, translation work and maintenance obligations. The OSCAL examples do not establish which boundary best supports interoperable hardening workflows.

questions.q: Where should rule metadata, including remediation, go?
questions.why: The DISA XCCDF benchmark carries the fields below, with distinct check and fix content. The AWS and DISA OSCAL examples use namespaced properties for severity rather than a dedicated field. The STIG and CIS assessment-plan examples include remediation as steps, but an AP step does not inherently distinguish a check from a fix; they rely on titles or step-type properties. Which metadata belongs in each OSCAL model, and how should consumers distinguish remediation from checks?

questions.q: What does an assessment-platform add when an assessment component already describes the runner?
questions.why: An OSCAL assessment plan can declare a runner as a component in assessment-assets, or describe an assessment-platform that includes a component. The examples do not establish what information the platform contributes beyond that component, such as execution context, or when that additional structure is needed. This choice applies regardless of where the hardening rule is modeled.

questions.q: How should an assessment plan associate an assessment asset with its tasks or activities?
questions.why: Assessment results can associate a task and the assessment-platform that produced its results, using result origins and actors to identify the producer. An assessment plan, however, has no corresponding way to instruct which component or assessment-platform should execute each task or activity before results exist. That plan-side linkage is needed across all three approaches, regardless of where the hardening rule is modeled.

sections.label: Catalog-first
sections.intro: The rule is a control in a catalog. Open questions concern how catalogs combine, how many documents that produces and where outcomes land.

questions.q: Do many catalogs converge into one profile and one plan of record, or does each catalog need its own?
questions.why: A single plan of record could answer a profile merging the catalogs that apply to a system. Separate plans could instead answer each catalog. These structures produce different file counts and response locations, and change whether benchmark outcomes sit beside regulatory outcomes. The worked scenario assumes convergence and counts 18 files; the question is whether that structure meets implementation and assessment needs.

questions.q: If OSCAL catalog controls gained a field for requirement level, how much of this disagreement would be left?
questions.why: OSCAL catalog controls have no dedicated core field distinguishing shall, should and may. The examples can carry such labels in properties, but consumers need conventions to interpret them. Catalog-first puts benchmark and regulatory controls into the same profile. It remains unclear how much model-placement disagreement concerns binding force rather than document structure, and whether a shared requirement-level field would reduce it.

questions.q: Should an OSCAL catalog control declare its type, so a regulatory control and a technical hardening control can be told apart?
questions.why: The catalog/profile model can combine regulatory controls with technical hardening controls, but it has no dedicated core field distinguishing those kinds. Tools would need a shared property convention or schema support to report regulatory coverage separately from hardening coverage. This question concerns the kind of requirement, distinct from whether its requirement level is shall, should or may.

questions.q: How should benchmark profiles compose with regulatory profiles as the number of controls grows?
questions.why: Combining benchmark and regulatory controls increases the work of resolving imports, selections, exclusions and parameter values. The question is how tools should compose and maintain those profiles at scale without obscuring which source supplied a requirement or how a tailoring decision changes downstream content.

questions.q: Where should benchmark outcomes be recorded, in SSP implementation claims or assessment results, and how should tools distinguish them?
questions.why: An SSP by-component response describes an implementation claim, while assessment results record evidence and outcomes. A benchmark workflow may need both, but they answer different questions. Tools need to distinguish intended configuration from observed satisfaction and preserve the relationship between the two records.

questions.q: How should evidence be linked to an SSP implementation claim when a benchmark result is recorded there?
questions.why: An assessment-results observation can use relevant-evidence to point to supporting material. An SSP by-component implementation claim has no equivalent field for attaching evidence directly to the claim. If a benchmark outcome is recorded in the SSP, how should tools connect that claim to its supporting evidence without conflating it with an assessed result in an AR?

questions.q: How should an SSP combine benchmark and vendor catalogs that describe the same system recommendations?
questions.why: A benchmark and a vendor catalog may describe overlapping recommendations for the same system. An SSP responding to both needs to preserve which source supplied each recommendation while avoiding duplicate or conflicting implementation claims. It remains open whether one profile should reconcile those controls before the SSP imports it, or whether another convention should relate equivalent recommendations.

sections.label: Component-first
sections.intro: The rule sits on the component it configures. Open questions concern importing component definitions and tailoring benchmark content.

questions.q: Which component definition carries the tie to the framework, the one holding the rules or the one holding the checks?
questions.why: The control link is inline rather than held in a mapping collection. The software component definition holds rules, while the validation component definition holds checks; those artifacts may have different maintainers. A mapping provider could update either or both. The OSCAL examples do not establish which document should own that relationship or how duplicated mappings would stay consistent.

questions.q: How should an SSP combine benchmark and vendor component definitions that describe the same system component?
questions.why: A system may use vendor component definitions alongside benchmark component definitions for the same software. Importing both can produce overlapping descriptions, rules and control implementations. It remains open whether an SSP should retain multiple OSCAL components, merge them, or use another convention to represent the single system component consistently.

questions.q: Which benchmark context should enter an SSP, and how should tools filter component-definition content during import?
questions.why: Benchmark content can include rules, parameters, rationale and procedural detail, not all of which serves the same purpose in an SSP. Import tooling needs a policy for retaining or omitting that context. The open issue is how to reduce duplication without losing information needed to interpret an implementation claim.

questions.q: How should component definitions support benchmark selection, exclusions and parameter tailoring?
questions.why: The component-first examples place parameters on proposed rules and set-parameters on control implementations. Those structures address parameter values but do not provide a profile's selection and exclusion workflow. How component definitions should support benchmark tailoring, including the scope and persistence of tailoring decisions, remains open.

questions.q: Should assessment plans or assessment results support importing component definitions with benchmark context?
questions.why: The component-first examples carry check content into an assessment plan through assessment assets. That demonstrates one encoding, not a dedicated import mechanism for all benchmark context. The question is whether plans or results should support such imports directly and which rules, parameters and provenance would need to survive.

sections.label: Assessment-first
sections.intro: The rule is an activity in an assessment plan. The open question concerns tailoring requirements without losing their assessment context.

questions.q: How should assessment-plan benchmarks support tailoring available through catalogs and profiles?
questions.why: OSCAL assessment-plan activities and steps have no parameter assembly, so the assessment-first examples place required values in text. Tailoring can therefore require editing procedural content rather than selecting controls or setting parameter values through a profile. The question is how to support reusable, auditable tailoring without losing the assessment workflow.
